problem: The original RNR-Map (a BEV grid of latent codes renderable via NeRF) works in simulation but loses information when averaging pixel codes per cell. It transfers poorly to real-world RGB-D with noisy depth, roll/pitch/z motion and different camera intrinsics. Its correlation-based localization is unstable and its optimization-based refinement is slow.
motivation: Real-robot image-goal navigation needs a map that embeds visual information well, plus fast and robust localization. Averaging all pixel latents equally mixes informative regions (edges, corners) with flat walls and drops z information when projecting to 2D. Rendering-based localization such as Loc-NeRF is too slow and unstable for real-time use.
key_idea: Improve RNR-Map with a learned per-pixel weighted projection, 3D positional encoding and a fixed focal length, then fuse its correlation heatmap with odometry in a particle filter (no rendering) to build a real-robot image-goal navigation system.
insight: Positional encoding gives most of the rendering gain (PSNR 16.3 to 19.0), while the weighted map adds a smaller gain on top (19.11 with both). A particle filter on top of correlation localization cuts distance error by about 59% (0.293 to 0.119 m) and raises RR to 97.1%, without any rendering. In real-world navigation, localization quality, not planning, dominated success: the original RNR-Map often mislocated start or goal.
method: Weighted map: the encoder outputs an extra per-pixel map B_t, weights beta = softmax(B_t) scale each latent before averaging per grid cell, and N stores the sum of weights; the weights peak at corners and edges.
Positional encoding: NeRF-style sin/cos encoding of each pixel's 3D world position is concatenated to the RGB-D input, preserving z information lost in 2D projection.
Generalizable input size: images are resized so fx=fy=128, so the same trained encoder and decoder work on real cameras (Kinect v1) with no fine-tuning.

Correlation-based localizer: U-Net key and query maps; the query map is rotated to 36 angles using weight-mask-aware interpolation (M⊙N)_r/N_r, then cross-correlated with the key map to give a pose heatmap.

Particle filter: particles (u,v,α) are weighted by the softmax-normalised heatmap, propagated with noisy odometry deltas, and the pose is a weighted mean (atan2 for orientation); no rendering is needed.

RNR-Nav system: the target pose is localized from the goal image on the prebuilt RNR-Map++, and the robot is tracked by localizer plus particle filter. The planner uses an occupancy map with obstacle-inflated safe regions, replans local paths, and stops within 30 cm of the goal.

setting.backbone: RNR-Map++ conv encoder + GSN-style NeRF decoder + U-Net correlation localizer (trained from scratch on ScanNet) + classical particle filter + occupancy-map path planner
setting.training_data: ScanNet, 500 of the 1500 training sequences; no real-robot fine-tuning
setting.action_space: 4 discrete actions: forward 25 cm, turn left 10°, turn right 10°, stop (goal distance < 30 cm)
setting.simulator: real world only (offline evaluation on ScanNet)
setting.privileged: a prebuilt RNR-Map++ and occupancy map of the environment (built from a prior tour with ORB-SLAM3 poses treated as GT) are given; goal image is RGB-D

numbers.extra: prebuilt map and occupancy map required; ORB-SLAM3 poses used as GT for map building; no fine-tuning on real data

results: RNR-Nav reaches 84.4% success (27/32) in real-world image-goal navigation versus 15.6% (5/32) for the original RNR-Map with optimization-based localization. Localization runs at 39.4 ms versus 248 ms. On ScanNet, RNR-Map++ with the particle filter beats Loc-NeRF (RR 44.3%) and RNR-Map (0.375 m error), and rendering PSNR improves from 16.3 to 19.1.
limitations: Requires a pre-built RNR-Map++ and occupancy map from a prior tour, with poses from ORB-SLAM3 and known camera intrinsics.
Performance drops in visually monotonous corridors (66.7% vs 95.0% in the laboratory), and failures include collisions in narrow passages.
Small real-world evaluation (32 trajectories, two environments, one robot), and the baseline is only the original RNR-Map.
